notes: Overall a solid implementation. Architectural adherence is strong: event bus is used for inter-service communication, each service owns its own data store, HTTP handling is confined to the router, and each service is in its own file. Key issues found: (1) The comment.added event payload includes 'assigneeId' in the notification handler subscription, but the CommentService publishes the payload without 'assigneeId' — it publishes 'authorId' instead. The NotificationService subscribes to 'comment.added' and uses payload.assigneeId, which will be undefined, meaning comment notifications are broken and will create notifications for undefined userId. This is a functional bug. (2) Forward-only status transition enforcement correctly throws an error, but the router catches this generically and returns 500 instead of 400, giving a poor API experience. (3) The demo script passes authorName and taskTitle as parameters to CommentService.create(), which leaks cross-service data knowledge into the HTTP layer — the router has to gather and pass task/user names, which slightly violates the spirit of service isolation (though no direct service-to-service calls are made). (4) Input validation is minimal throughout — no checks for missing required fields (name, email, title, etc.), which could cause silent failures or malformed records. (5) The UserService.update() spreads all updates including potentially overwriting the id field, though it does re-apply id afterwards. (6) Email uniqueness is not enforced. (7) The status transition equality case (same status) is silently allowed and fires a statusChanged event with oldStatus === newStatus, which is a minor logic issue. (8) No unsubscribe mechanism on EventBus. (9) The dist/ files are only declaration files, indicating the source is TypeScript-compiled — acceptable. Constraint compliance is high: no external npm dependencies for app code, Node built-in http module used, forward-only transitions implemented, event bus present, services separated. The comment notification bug is the most significant functional defect.
